title: From gross potential rent to stabilised NOI
summary: The revenue side of a pro forma is a staircase from the rent a full building could charge down to the net operating income it actually keeps. This lesson walks each step, defines the three terms that matter, and shows why a small rent error becomes a larger value error.
body:
Value is built from net operating income, and net operating income is built from rent. Get the rent wrong by 5 percent and you can get the value wrong by more than that, because costs do not fall when rent does.

Recall

Q. Why must a budget handed to a lender state its basis, assumptions and exclusions?

A. Because once someone relies on it, it is a representation. Disclosure of what the number is, and is not, is what makes it defensible; a general disclaimer is not enough.

Q. In owner accounting, what is accrual accounting?

A. Recording revenue when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, not when cash moves. Rent for March is March revenue even if the tenant pays in April.

Q. What is the purpose of a one-page memo?

A. To put the conclusion and its support on one page so a decision-maker can act without a meeting.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week you built the cost side of the pro forma: what the building costs. This week is the other side: what it earns. A developer's profit is the gap between what a completed building is worth and what it cost, and what it is worth is driven almost entirely by its income. A lender sizes the permanent loan on income. An appraiser values the building on income. A buyer prices it on income. If you understand each step from rent to net operating income, you can test anyone's pro forma in minutes and see which line is doing the heavy lifting.

The staircase

Picture a staircase that steps down from the most a building could ever collect to what the owner actually keeps. Each step has a name.

  1. Gross potential rent (GPR). The rent the building would collect in a year if every unit were leased at market rent and every tenant paid. It is a ceiling, not a forecast.
  2. Other income. Parking, storage, laundry, pet fees. Small lines, but real.
  3. Potential gross income. Gross potential rent plus other income.
  4. Vacancy and credit loss. The income lost because some units are empty between tenants and some tenants do not pay. It is deducted as a percentage.
  5. Effective gross income (EGI). What the building actually collects: potential gross income minus vacancy and credit loss.
  6. Operating expenses. The cost of running the building: property tax, insurance, utilities in common areas, repairs and maintenance, staff and the property management fee.
  7. Replacement reserve. An annual amount set aside for items that wear out, such as roofs, boilers and appliances. Practice varies on whether it sits above or below the net operating income line, but lenders usually deduct it, so do so in your underwriting.
  8. Net operating income (NOI). Effective gross income minus operating expenses and reserves. It excludes loan payments, income tax and depreciation. It is the income the property earns, regardless of how it is financed or owned.

Be just as clear about what NOI leaves out. It does not deduct loan payments, because it measures the property, not the owner's financing. It does not deduct income tax, because tax depends on who owns it and how. It does not deduct depreciation, an accounting allocation of cost that involves no cash. And it does not normally deduct major one-off capital spending, such as replacing all the windows, or the leasing commissions paid to find tenants, though careful underwriters show those separately below NOI. When someone quotes you an NOI, ask what has been deducted and what has not; two people can mean different things by the same three letters.

Stabilised NOI is the NOI once the building has finished leasing up and is operating normally, at its long-run occupancy, with no temporary discounts. It is the number a pro forma is ultimately trying to predict, and it is the number every valuation rests on.

Worked example: the 60-unit building

All numbers are hypothetical. The building has 60 apartments. Market rent, supported by signed leases at comparable buildings, is 2,750 a month.

LineCalculationAnnual
Gross potential rent60 × 2,750 × 121,980,000
Other income30 parking stalls × 100 × 12, plus 24,000 storage and laundry60,000
Potential gross income1,980,000 + 60,0002,040,000
Vacancy and credit loss5 percent of 2,040,000(102,000)
Effective gross income2,040,000 − 102,0001,938,000
Operating expenses8,500 per unit × 60(510,000)
Replacement reserve300 per unit × 60(18,000)
Stabilised NOI1,938,000 − 528,0001,410,000

If similar stabilised buildings sell at a capitalisation rate of 5.0 percent, meaning buyers pay a price at which NOI is 5 percent of the price, the value is 1,410,000 ÷ 0.05 = 28,200,000. Against last week's total cost of 23,500,000, yield on cost is 1,410,000 ÷ 23,500,000 = 6.0 percent, and the development profit is 4,700,000.

Say that out loud now.

Why a rent error grows

Second worked example. Suppose the real market rent is 5 percent lower, 2,612.50 a month, because the comparable leases you relied on included a premium corner building. Rework the staircase.

  • Gross potential rent: 1,980,000 × 0.95 = 1,881,000.
  • Potential gross income: 1,881,000 + 60,000 = 1,941,000.
  • Vacancy at 5 percent: 97,050. Effective gross income: 1,843,950.
  • Expenses and reserves are unchanged at 528,000. NOI: 1,843,950 − 528,000 = 1,315,950.
  • Value at 5.0 percent: 26,319,000.

Rent fell 5 percent. NOI fell 94,050, which is 6.7 percent. Value fell 1,881,000, also 6.7 percent. And the development profit fell from 4,700,000 to 2,819,000, a drop of 40 percent. That is the operating leverage of a building: expenses are largely fixed, so every lost dollar of rent comes straight off NOI, and profit is a thin slice on top of a large cost. A small revenue error is never small for the developer.

How the best do it

The disciplined institutional owners and lenders share a practice worth copying: they underwrite effective rent, not asking rent. Asking rent is what a landlord advertises. Effective rent is what tenants actually pay after concessions such as free months, spread across the lease. They build their rent assumption from a rent roll, meaning the list of every unit, tenant, lease date and rent actually paid, in comparable buildings, and they adjust each comparable for size, floor, view, age and amenities. A small developer can copy this with a spreadsheet: ten comparable leases, actual signed rents where you can get them, each adjusted and dated. When a lender asks where your rent came from, you hand them that sheet.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the rent assumption is the softest number in the pro forma and the one with the largest effect. Costs come from quotes; rent often comes from a broker's optimism. The control is an independent rent study, or your own comparable lease sheet, with effective rents, dated, and a sensitivity line on the pro forma showing value and profit at rent 5 percent lower.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner calculates value from gross potential rent, or forgets that vacancy applies even to a well-run building. A full building is not a stabilised building. Every apartment turns over, and the days between tenants are lost income every year.

Callback

In Week 10 you learned that value equals NOI divided by the capitalisation rate. Today you built the numerator. Last week you built the denominator of yield on cost. Put the two weeks together and the whole development equation is on one page: what it costs, what it earns, what it is worth, and the margin between them.

Recap

The revenue staircase runs from gross potential rent, plus other income, minus vacancy and credit loss to effective gross income, minus operating expenses and reserves to stabilised net operating income. Value is stabilised NOI divided by the cap rate. Because expenses are largely fixed, a small rent error becomes a larger NOI, value and profit error. Underwrite effective rent from signed comparables.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on a famous acquisition whose revenue plan depended on rents the law would not allow.
checklist: Start revenue from gross potential rent at supported market rent
Add other income only where it is evidenced
Deduct vacancy and credit loss even for a strong building
Include the property management fee in operating expenses
Deduct a replacement reserve as lenders do
Underwrite effective rent after concessions, not asking rent
Keep a dated sheet of comparable signed leases with adjustments
Show value and profit at rent 5 percent lower
head: Field checklist
speak: Revenue is a staircase. Gross potential rent is what a full building would collect at market rent. Add other income such as parking and storage to get potential gross income. Subtract vacancy and credit loss, because units turn over and some tenants don't pay, to get effective gross income. Subtract operating expenses, including property tax, insurance, repairs, staff and management, and a reserve for things that wear out, to get net operating income. Stabilised NOI is that number once the building is fully leased and running normally. On a hypothetical 60-unit building at 2,750 a month, stabilised NOI is 1.41 million, worth 28.2 million at a 5 percent cap rate. If rent is 5 percent lower, NOI and value fall 6.7 percent and development profit falls 40 percent, because expenses don't fall with rent. So I underwrite effective rent from signed comparables, dated, with a sensitivity line beside it.
terms: Gross potential rent — the annual rent a building would collect if every unit were leased at market rent and every tenant paid.
Effective gross income — potential gross income minus vacancy and credit loss; what the building actually collects.
Stabilised net operating income — net operating income once a building has finished leasing up and operates normally at long-run occupancy.

hostile.q: Your rent is 2,750. The building down the street is advertising 2,600. Why are you right?
hostile.a: Because I am not comparing to an advertised rent; I am comparing to signed leases. My sheet has ten comparable leases, dated within six months, adjusted for size, floor and age, and the effective rent after concessions averages within a few percent of 2,750. The building down the street is older and has no parking, and I have its effective rent on the sheet. I also show you value and profit at 5 percent lower rent, so you can see the deal still works if I am wrong.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman on finance
title: Stuyvesant Town: revenue the law would not allow
summary: In 2006 a buyer paid a record price for a large Manhattan rental complex on a plan to lift regulated rents to market. Courts, credit markets and the rent law intervened, and the owners handed control to lenders in 2010. This lesson takes the case through seven steps.
body:
The Stuyvesant Town purchase did not fail because the buildings were poor or the location was weak. It failed because the revenue line depended on rents the owners did not yet have the right to charge.

Recall

Q. Why is construction interest a circular calculation?

A. Because interest is usually paid from the loan, so the loan must grow to cover it, which creates more interest. It must be solved by iteration, not deleted.

Q. What is work in progress in owner accounting?

A. Costs incurred on an asset not yet complete, carried on the balance sheet until the asset is finished.

Q. What is the three-step answer to a hostile question?

A. Acknowledge, bridge to what matters, then answer directly with evidence.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a revenue assumption that depends on a change you do not control is not a forecast. It is a bet. Stuyvesant Town is the clearest large example of a bet on revenue placed in the base case of a pro forma. The facts below are drawn from contemporaneous reporting and the court record. Verify specific figures against those sources before you cite them.

Step 1: Timeline

  • Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village are adjacent rental complexes in Manhattan, together roughly eleven thousand apartments, built in the 1940s.
  • 2006: The long-time owner, an insurance company, sells the complexes. A partnership led by Tishman Speyer with BlackRock buys them for about 5.4 billion dollars, a record price for a residential property at the time, financed largely with debt.
  • Most units were rent-stabilised, meaning their rents could rise only within limits set under New York's rent laws. The business plan relied on moving many units to market rents over time as they became eligible.
  • 2007 to 2009: Rental markets and credit markets weaken in the financial crisis.
  • 2009: New York's highest court rules, in a case brought by tenants and known as Roberts v. Tishman Speyer, that owners receiving a particular property tax benefit could not take units out of rent stabilisation while receiving it.
  • 2010: The owners default and hand control of the property to their lenders.

Step 2: Key decisions

The decisive choices were to pay a price that only worked if regulated rents moved to market rents, and to finance that price with heavy debt whose service the existing rents could not cover. Reserves were set aside to fund the shortfall until rents rose. That is a structure in which time is the enemy: every month the conversion was slower than planned, the reserves shrank.

Step 3: Assumptions

Three assumptions carried the price. First, that units could be deregulated at a planned pace. Second, that market rents for converted units would keep rising. Third, that the legal framework, including how a tax benefit interacted with deregulation, would permit the plan. The third assumption was a legal judgement embedded in a revenue line, and it was not shown as a separate risk.

Step 4: Incentives

In a competitive auction the winning bid is often the one with the most optimistic assumptions, which economists call the winner's curse. Lenders in that period were packaging and selling loans to other investors, which can weaken the incentive to scrutinise the underwriting closely. And a sponsor who earns fees on a transaction is rewarded for closing it.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The clearest warning sign was structural: in-place income did not cover debt service on day one, and the gap was funded from reserves. A second sign was that the plan depended on tenant turnover in a community where long tenure was common and tenants were organised. A third was legal: questions about how the tax benefit affected the right to deregulate were being raised and litigated. Each of these was knowable before the closing.

Step 6: Point of no return

Once the court ruled, the deregulation already done was in question and the planned pace could not continue. With reserves depleting and market rents softening at the same time, there was no path to cover debt service from operations. From that point the outcome was decided by the lenders' rights, not the owners' plan.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was a base-case revenue line that included income the owners did not have the legal right to collect at the time of purchase, financed with debt that assumed the income would arrive on schedule. The upside was priced as if it were certain, and the leverage removed any room for it to arrive late.

What a careful buyer would have done

Run the counterfactual. A careful buyer of the same asset could still have bid, but on a different structure. First, price the base case: the value supported by in-place rents and the increases current rules plainly allowed. Second, finance the base case: debt sized so that in-place income covered debt service with a margin, so that time was not the enemy. Third, treat the deregulation plan as an option: something that adds value if it works and costs only the effort if it does not. Fourth, obtain a legal opinion on the specific question of how the tax benefit interacted with deregulation, and treat any doubt in that opinion as a reason to exclude the income. Such a buyer would probably have lost the auction. That is the point. Sometimes the disciplined outcome of a competitive bid is to lose it, and the winner's curse lands on someone else.

Translating it to a small project

Worked example, hypothetical. You are buying a 20-unit regulated building for 6,000,000. In-place rents total 480,000 of NOI. You model NOI rising to 600,000 within three years by raising rents as units turn over. At a 5 percent cap rate, 480,000 supports a value of 9,600,000 and 600,000 supports 12,000,000. You borrow 4,500,000 at an annual debt service of 360,000. Today's debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), NOI divided by annual debt payments, is 480,000 ÷ 360,000 = 1.33. That is survivable. Now suppose instead you had paid 8,000,000 and borrowed 6,000,000 at 480,000 a year of debt service, because the planned NOI justified it. DSCR on in-place income is 480,000 ÷ 480,000 = 1.00. Any vacancy, any repair, any delay in the rent plan, and you are funding the loan from your own pocket. Same building. The difference is whether the price and the debt were sized to income you have or income you hope for.

Second worked example. Show the plan honestly as two lines. Base case: in-place rents with only increases the current rules allow, NOI 480,000. Upside case: the turnover plan, NOI 600,000. Price and debt are sized to the base case. The upside is the reason to buy, not the reason the deal works.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is legal and regulatory risk hidden inside a revenue line, where it looks like a market assumption. The control is to tag every revenue assumption with its source: market evidence, contract, or a change in law, regulation or tenancy that has not yet happened. Only the first two belong in the base case.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner pays for the upside. A seller will always describe the upside; the buyer's discipline is to pay for the base case and treat the upside as the reward for doing the work.

Rule 14

I underwrite revenue only from rents I can legally charge and have evidence tenants pay today; any increase that depends on a change in law, regulation or tenancy is shown as upside, never as base case.

Callback

In Week 7 you learned about a liquidity floor: the cash you never let your personal balance sheet fall below. Reserves in a deal are the project's liquidity floor. At Stuyvesant Town, the reserves were sized to a timetable, and when the timetable broke, the floor broke with it. Size reserves to a delay, not to a plan.

Recap

A record price was paid for a regulated complex on a plan to convert rents to market, financed with debt the existing income could not cover. A court ruling, a market downturn and depleting reserves ended it, and the lenders took control. Rule 14: base-case revenue comes only from rents you can legally charge and can evidence today.

Next: Roman on how a lender underwrites your stabilised NOI and why its number is lower than yours.
checklist: Tag each revenue assumption: market evidence, contract, or change not yet happened
Put only market evidence and contract in the base case
Check current rent regulation and tenancy rules before underwriting increases
Size price and debt to in-place or base-case income
Confirm debt service is covered by in-place income on day one
Size reserves for delay, not for the plan's timetable
Show upside as a separate line with its own risks named
head: Field checklist
speak: In 2006 a partnership paid about 5.4 billion dollars for Stuyvesant Town and Peter Cooper Village, roughly eleven thousand mostly rent-stabilised apartments in Manhattan. The price only worked if many units moved to market rents, and heavy debt meant existing rents did not cover debt service, so reserves filled the gap. Then the financial crisis softened rents, and in 2009 New York's highest court ruled that owners receiving a particular tax benefit could not deregulate units while receiving it. Reserves ran down and in 2010 the owners handed control to lenders. The root cause was a base case that counted income the owners did not yet have the legal right to collect, with leverage that left no room for delay. My rule is Rule 14: I underwrite revenue only from rents I can legally charge and have evidence tenants pay today; anything that depends on a change in law, regulation or tenancy is upside, never base case.
terms: Rent stabilisation — a form of rent regulation that limits how much and how often rents on covered units can rise.
Winner's curse — the tendency for the winning bidder in a competitive auction to be the one with the most optimistic, and often overpriced, assumptions.
In-place income — the income a property actually earns today from its existing leases, as opposed to projected income.

hostile.q: Your pro forma shows rents rising 25 percent over three years. How much of that is legally available to you today?
hostile.a: The base case shows only the increases the current rules allow on existing tenancies, and the price and the debt are sized to that case; debt service is covered on in-place income at 1.33 times. The 25 percent is the upside case, shown on a separate line, and it depends on turnover and on rent rules that I have had reviewed by counsel. If none of it happens, the deal still services its debt. That is the point of the structure.

rule: Rule 14: I underwrite revenue only from rents I can legally charge and have evidence tenants pay today; any increase that depends on a change in law, regulation or tenancy is shown as upside, never as base case.

title: The lender's NOI is lower than yours
summary: A lender does not size a permanent loan on your stabilised NOI. It builds its own, with higher vacancy, its own rent and its own reserves, then applies coverage tests. This lesson shows how that gap creates a refinance shortfall and what it means for your balance sheet.
body:
Your pro forma shows what the building should earn. The lender's underwriting shows what it is prepared to believe. The difference between the two is cash you will have to find at refinance.

Recall

Q. What does an interest reserve do?

A. It sets aside part of the loan to pay the loan's own interest until the building earns enough to cover it.

Q. Why do owners keep a reporting pack each month?

A. To show budget, cost to date, committed cost and forecast together, so problems are seen while they can still be fixed.

Q. What is the danger of answering a number you have not checked?

A. A wrong number spoken confidently is remembered, and correcting it later costs more trust than saying "I'll confirm by Friday."

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most rental developments are built with a construction loan that must be repaid when the building is finished and leased. It is usually repaid by a permanent loan, often called a take-out loan, from the same or another lender. That permanent loan is sized on stabilised NOI. If the lender's NOI is lower than yours, the take-out is smaller than the construction loan it must repay, and the difference comes from you. Developers who do not model this find out in the last month of the project, when there is no time left to raise money cheaply. Equity raised in a hurry, against a maturing loan, is the most expensive money a developer ever takes, because every party at the table knows you have no alternative.

How a lender rebuilds your NOI

A lender's underwriter takes your pro forma and replaces your assumptions with its own. The adjustments are commercial practice, not standards, and they vary by lender and market, but they follow a pattern.

  • Rent. The lower of your rent, in-place rents, or the lender's appraiser's market rent.
  • Vacancy. The higher of your vacancy, the market's actual vacancy, or the lender's floor, often several points above zero even in a tight market.
  • Expenses. The higher of your budget, historical expenses for comparable buildings, or the lender's minimums, including a management fee even if you plan to manage it yourself.
  • Reserves. The lender's own figure per unit, usually higher than a developer's.

Worked example, hypothetical. Your stabilised NOI on a 60-unit building is 1,410,000: rent 2,750 a month, 5 percent vacancy, operating expenses 510,000 and reserves of 300 per unit. The lender's appraiser concludes market rent is 2,650. The lender uses 7 percent vacancy and 400 per unit of reserves.

  1. Gross potential rent: 60 × 2,650 × 12 = 1,908,000.
  2. Plus other income of 60,000: potential gross income 1,968,000.
  3. Vacancy at 7 percent: 137,760. Effective gross income: 1,830,240.
  4. Operating expenses 510,000 and reserves 24,000: NOI = 1,830,240 − 534,000 = 1,296,240.

The lender's NOI is about 114,000 lower than yours, roughly 8 percent, from three adjustments none of which sounds dramatic on its own.

Say that out loud now.

Sizing the take-out loan

The lender now applies coverage tests. The most common is the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), NOI divided by annual principal and interest. Suppose the lender requires 1.25 times, which is commercial practice and varies. The maximum annual debt service is 1,296,240 ÷ 1.25 = 1,036,992.

To turn annual debt service into a loan amount, use the mortgage constant: annual payment divided by loan amount for an amortising loan. For a hypothetical 6 percent interest rate amortised over 25 years with monthly payments, the constant is about 7.73 percent. Your lender or a financial calculator gives it exactly. Maximum loan: 1,036,992 ÷ 0.0773 ≈ 13,415,000.

A second test is debt yield: NOI divided by the loan amount, which ignores interest rates altogether. If the lender wants a 9 percent debt yield, again a hypothetical practice figure, the maximum loan is 1,296,240 ÷ 0.09 = 14,402,667. The lender takes the lower of the two. Here DSCR binds, at about 13,415,000.

Second worked example: the gap. The construction loan to be repaid is 15,275,000. The take-out is about 13,415,000. The refinance shortfall is about 1,860,000. On your own NOI of 1,410,000, the same tests would have supported 1,410,000 ÷ 1.25 ÷ 0.0773 ≈ 14,592,000, so even your optimistic case leaves a gap of nearly 700,000. The project needs more equity at the end, or a period of seasoning while rents rise, or a lender willing to accept a lower coverage, at a higher price.

Each assumption has a price in loan dollars

It helps to translate each lender adjustment into the loan amount it costs, because that tells you where to spend your effort. At a 1.25 times coverage and a 7.73 percent constant, every dollar of NOI supports about 1 ÷ 1.25 ÷ 0.0773 = 10.35 dollars of loan. One percentage point of vacancy on potential gross income of 1,968,000 is 19,680 of NOI, which is about 204,000 of loan. Each 10 dollars of monthly rent across 60 units is 7,200 of annual rent, which after 7 percent vacancy is 6,696 of NOI and about 69,000 of loan. Each 100 dollars a unit of extra reserves is 6,000 of NOI and about 62,000 of loan. Seen this way, the appraiser's rent is worth arguing with evidence, the vacancy assumption is worth supporting with the market's actual data, and the reserve figure is rarely worth a fight. Spend your credibility where the loan dollars are.

What it does to the deal

The shortfall changes the economics in two ways. First, the developer's equity stays in the deal longer and in greater amount, which lowers its return, a subject for next week. Second, the refinance date becomes a cliff: the construction loan matures on a fixed date, and if the shortfall is not covered by then, the lender can declare a default. The control is to model the take-out at the lender's NOI from the first day of underwriting, and to negotiate an extension option on the construction loan as insurance.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note for your personal balance sheet. A refinance shortfall is a future call on cash with a known date. If you have guaranteed any part of the construction loan, that call can land on you personally. Record the modelled shortfall, at the lender's NOI, as a planned use of your liquidity, and hold the cash, or a committed source for it, before the building is finished. Profit on paper does not repay a maturing loan. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any personal financial decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the take-out will equal the construction loan. The control is a refinance test in the pro forma using the lender's likely rent, vacancy and reserves, the required coverage and a mortgage constant, with the shortfall shown as a line in sources and uses.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sizes the permanent loan on their own NOI at the loan-to-value ratio they hope for. Lenders lend on the binding constraint, and for income property that is usually coverage, not value. On this building, 65 percent of a 28,200,000 value would be 18,330,000, a figure no coverage test here supports. Run every test and take the lowest answer, because that is what the lender will do.

Callback

In Week 13 you saw that once a construction loan is committed, cost overruns fall on equity. The refinance shortfall is the same principle at the other end of the project. The debt is fixed at both ends by tests you do not control, and equity absorbs the difference both times.

Recap

A lender rebuilds your NOI with the lower rent, the higher vacancy and expenses, and larger reserves. It then sizes the take-out loan on the binding test, usually DSCR. On this building, an 8 percent lower NOI produced a 1.86 million refinance shortfall. Model it from day one and hold the cash for it.

Next: REGA on the laws and rules that govern rent and operating costs.
checklist: Rebuild your NOI the way a lender will: lower rent, higher vacancy, management fee, higher reserves
Apply the lender's DSCR test with a mortgage constant
Apply the debt yield test and take the lower loan
Compare the take-out loan with the construction loan to be repaid
Show any refinance shortfall as a line in sources and uses
Negotiate an extension option on the construction loan
Record the shortfall as a planned use of personal liquidity if you have guaranteed debt
head: Field checklist
speak: A lender does not size a permanent loan on my NOI. It rebuilds its own: the lower of my rent or its appraiser's, higher vacancy, a management fee, and bigger reserves. On a hypothetical 60-unit building, my NOI is 1.41 million; the lender's is about 1.30 million, roughly 8 percent lower. It then applies coverage. At 1.25 times debt service coverage and a mortgage constant of about 7.7 percent, that NOI supports a take-out loan of about 13.4 million. But the construction loan to be repaid is 15.3 million. The refinance shortfall is about 1.86 million, and it comes from equity or a guarantor, on a fixed date. So I model the take-out at the lender's NOI from day one, show the shortfall in sources and uses, negotiate an extension option, and hold the cash before the building is finished.
terms: Take-out loan — the permanent loan that repays a construction loan once the building is complete and stabilised.
Mortgage constant — the annual principal and interest payment divided by the loan amount, for an amortising loan.
Debt yield — net operating income divided by the loan amount, a coverage test that ignores the interest rate.

hostile.q: Your pro forma assumes a 15.3 million take-out. Our numbers support 13.4. How do you close the gap?
hostile.a: Our model already uses your numbers for the take-out, not ours, so the gap is in our sources and uses as a 1.86 million line. It is covered by an equity commitment that funds at stabilisation, and the construction loan has a six-month extension option so we are not refinancing on a cliff. If rents prove stronger than your appraiser's, we refinance higher later; if not, the equity is already committed.

title: The rules that cap rent and raise costs
summary: Revenue and operating costs are shaped by rules: rent regulation, residential tenancy law, short-term rental restrictions and property tax assessment. This lesson explains each as a concept, without jurisdictional conclusions, and shows how to test a pro forma against them.
body:
A pro forma's revenue and expense lines are not only market questions. They are shaped by rules the developer does not control, and those rules should be checked before the numbers are believed.

Recall

Q. What does gross potential rent mean?

A. The annual rent a building would collect if every unit were leased at market rent and every tenant paid. It is a ceiling, not a forecast.

Q. What is a capitalised cost in owner accounting?

A. A cost recorded as part of the asset's value on the balance sheet rather than expensed in the period.

Q. What does "I'll confirm by Friday" protect?

A. Your credibility. It replaces a guess with a commitment, and delivering on it builds trust.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on Day 2 you saw a revenue plan fail because the law did not allow the rents it assumed. That is the extreme case. The everyday case is quieter: a rent growth rate the local rules do not permit, a short-term rental strategy a bylaw prohibits, or a property tax bill that doubles when the completed building is assessed. Each changes NOI, and through NOI, value. This lesson teaches what to check. It does not tell you what any jurisdiction's rules are. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer licensed in the jurisdiction, and for property tax, an assessment or tax adviser.

Rent regulation

Rent regulation is any rule that limits rent levels or rent increases on residential units. It takes different forms. Some systems cap the annual increase on a sitting tenant at a published guideline. Some allow the rent to reset to market between tenants, called vacancy decontrol, and some do not. Some exempt buildings first occupied after a certain date. Some apply only to certain building types. The details matter enormously and change over time, so check them for the specific property and date.

Worked example, hypothetical. Your pro forma grows rent 5 percent a year from 2,750. Suppose the jurisdiction caps annual increases on sitting tenants at a hypothetical 2 percent, and most tenants stay. After four years:

  • At 5 percent: 2,750 × 1.05⁴ = 2,750 × 1.2155 = 3,342.64 a month.
  • At 2 percent: 2,750 × 1.02⁴ = 2,750 × 1.0824 = 2,976.69 a month.
  • Difference: 365.95 a month per unit. Across 60 units for a year: 365.95 × 60 × 12 = 263,484.

That is about 263,000 of annual NOI the pro forma counted and the rules would not allow. At a 5 percent capitalisation rate it is about 5,270,000 of value. Even if the building is exempt today, check whether exemptions have been narrowed before, because a rule that changed once can change again.

Say that out loud now.

Residential tenancy law

Residential tenancy law governs the relationship between landlord and tenant: how leases are formed, what notice is needed to raise rent or end a tenancy, what deposits can be taken, how disputes are heard, and what the landlord must maintain. It affects revenue in three practical ways. First, notice periods delay rent increases. Second, the grounds and process for ending a tenancy affect how quickly a non-paying tenant can be replaced, which drives your credit loss assumption. Third, limits on deposits affect how much protection you hold against damage and arrears. When you set a vacancy and credit loss figure, ask how long it takes, under the local process, to recover a unit from a tenant who stops paying.

Credit loss is where tenancy law turns into a number. Hypothetically, if recovering a unit from a non-paying tenant takes four months under the local process, and one tenancy in fifty a year ends that way, the building loses about four months of rent on 60 ÷ 50 = 1.2 units a year: 1.2 × 4 × 2,750 = 13,200, before legal costs and the turnover period. That is a small line on its own, but it should come from the process, not from a habit.

Short-term rental and use restrictions

Many municipalities restrict short-term rentals of residential units, often by requiring a licence, limiting them to a principal residence, or prohibiting them in certain zones. A pro forma that assumes nightly rates on some units is assuming a use permission. Confirm it in the zoning and licensing rules for that address, and in any condominium declaration if the building is a condominium. A use the rules forbid has a revenue of zero, whatever the market would pay.

Other income is rule-bound too

The small lines in other income are often the most regulated per dollar. Rules in some places limit or prohibit application fees, cap or forbid certain pet charges, restrict how utility costs can be re-billed to tenants through sub-metering, or require parking to be bundled with a unit rather than charged separately. Late-payment charges may be capped. Hypothetically, a pro forma that carries 24,000 a year of fees and charges that the local rules do not permit has overstated NOI by 24,000 and value, at a 5 percent capitalisation rate, by 480,000. That is a lot of value from a line nobody looked at. The control is simple: for each other-income line, name the rule that permits it at that address, and if you cannot, leave it out of the base case until a lawyer confirms it.

Property tax assessment

Property tax is usually the largest single operating expense in a rental building. It is generally calculated as an assessed value, set by a public assessor, multiplied by a tax rate set by the taxing authority. During construction, the assessment often reflects land or a partly built structure. After completion, the building is reassessed, and the tax rises.

Second worked example, hypothetical. The pro forma carries property tax of 150,000 inside operating expenses of 510,000, based on the tax paid during construction. After completion, the assessor values the building at 24,000,000. At a hypothetical rate of 1 percent of assessed value, the annual tax is 240,000. NOI falls by 90,000, from 1,410,000 to 1,320,000. At a 5 percent capitalisation rate, value falls by 1,800,000. One line, set from the wrong year's bill, removed more than a third of the development profit on a project where profit was 4,700,000.

The control is to estimate property tax on the completed building's likely assessed value, using the assessor's published method where available, and to ask an adviser whether the jurisdiction allows appeals, phase-ins or incentives for new rental housing. Do not assume any of them exist.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating rule-driven lines as market lines. Rent growth, credit loss, unit use and property tax are all partly set by public rules. The control is a one-page rules check for each project: rent regulation status and history, tenancy process timelines, permitted uses including short-term rental, and the completed-building property tax estimate, each with its source and date.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner copies the property tax line from the seller's or the construction-period bill. An existing building's tax reflects its current assessment; a new building's tax will reflect its completed value. The same mistake appears with insurance: a construction-period builder's risk premium says nothing about the operating policy the finished building will need, which a broker should price before the pro forma is shared.

Callback

In Week 13 you learned that a budget shared with a lender is a representation. The same applies to revenue. If your pro forma assumes rent growth or a use that you know, or should know, the rules do not permit, the forecast carries an implied statement that it is reasonable. The rules check is how you make that statement true.

Recap

Rent regulation can cap increases and keep rents below market. Tenancy law sets the timelines behind vacancy and credit loss. Use restrictions can make a revenue line zero. Property tax rises when the completed building is assessed. Check each, with sources, and verify against primary sources before relying on them.

Next: Sage reverse engineers a pro forma, starting from the value a lender needs and working back to the rent and the lease-up pace required.
checklist: Confirm whether rent regulation applies to the property, and how it has changed before
Grow rent only at rates the applicable rules permit for sitting tenants
Check notice periods and tenancy recovery timelines before setting credit loss
Confirm any short-term rental or special use is permitted at the address
Estimate property tax on the completed building's likely assessed value
Ask an adviser about appeals, phase-ins or incentives; assume none
Keep a one-page rules check with sources and dates for each project
head: Field checklist
speak: Revenue and costs are shaped by rules, not only markets. Rent regulation can cap annual increases; on a hypothetical 60-unit building, growing rent at 5 percent a year when the rules allow 2 percent overstates annual income by about 263,000 after four years, worth over 5 million at a 5 percent cap rate. Tenancy law sets how long it takes to replace a non-paying tenant, which drives credit loss. Use restrictions can make a short-term rental line worth zero. And property tax usually jumps when the completed building is reassessed; a tax line copied from the construction-period bill can understate expenses by 90,000 a year and value by 1.8 million. So I keep a one-page rules check on every project, with sources and dates, and I verify each point against the primary source with a lawyer and a tax adviser before I rely on it.
terms: Rent regulation — rules that limit rent levels or annual rent increases on covered residential units.
Residential tenancy law — the rules governing leases, notices, deposits, rent increases and ending tenancies between landlords and residential tenants.
Assessed value — the value a public assessor assigns to a property for calculating property tax.

hostile.q: Your property tax line is 150,000. The building next door, which is smaller, pays more. Explain.
hostile.a: You're right to flag it, and the 150,000 was the construction-period figure. The revised pro forma estimates tax on the completed building's likely assessed value using the assessor's published method, which brings it to about 240,000, and NOI to 1.32 million. That revision is in the version I sent this morning, with the value and coverage tests re-run on it.

title: Reverse engineering the rent and the lease-up
summary: Start from the finished outcome and work backward: the value a lender needs, the NOI that supports it, the rent that produces that NOI, and the lease-up pace that gets there before the loan matures. A step-by-step calculation with units.
body:
The fastest way to test a pro forma is to run it backward. Start from the value the deal needs, work back to the rent required, then check whether the market and the calendar can deliver it.

Recall

Q. In a sources and uses table, what is gross floor area?

A. The total built floor area measured to the outside of the walls, including corridors and service space. Cost rates are usually applied to it, not to net area.

Q. What does a schedule of values do?

A. It breaks a contract sum into line items so progress and payment can be measured item by item.

Q. How should numbers be presented aloud?

A. In short sentences, one number at a time, with a pause after each so the listener can hold it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a forward pro forma starts with rent and ends with value, and every assumption along the way can be nudged until the answer looks right. Reverse engineering removes that temptation. You start with the outcome the deal must achieve and ask what has to be true. If the required rent is above anything the market has signed, or the required lease-up pace is faster than any comparable building achieved, you know before you spend a dollar. All numbers below are hypothetical.

Part 1: From the required value back to rent

The deal needs a completed value of 28,200,000 to deliver its target development profit on a cost of 23,500,000. Comparable stabilised buildings trade at a 5.0 percent capitalisation rate. Work backward.

  1. Required NOI. Value × cap rate = 28,200,000 × 0.05 = 1,410,000 a year.
  2. Add back expenses and reserves. Operating expenses are 510,000 (8,500 per unit) and reserves 18,000 (300 per unit). Required effective gross income = 1,410,000 + 528,000 = 1,938,000.
  3. Gross up for vacancy and credit loss. At 5 percent, effective gross income is 95 percent of potential gross income. Required potential gross income = 1,938,000 ÷ 0.95 = 2,040,000.
  4. Remove other income. Parking, storage and laundry produce 60,000. Required gross potential rent = 2,040,000 − 60,000 = 1,980,000.
  5. Convert to a monthly rent per unit. 1,980,000 ÷ 60 units ÷ 12 months = 2,750 a month.

So the question is not "what rent do we think we can get?" It is "can we evidence 2,750 a month in effective rent?" Go to the comparable lease sheet. If the best signed effective rents for similar units are 2,600, the deal does not work as priced, and no amount of forward modelling will change that.

Say that out loud now.

Notice that this method makes every assumption visible in one pass. Expenses, reserves, vacancy, other income and the cap rate each appear as a single step, and you can ask of each one: where did this come from, and what if it is wrong? Forward models hide that question inside a spreadsheet.

Part 2: From effective rent back to face rent

New buildings often lease up with concessions, such as a free month on a twelve-month lease. Effective rent is face rent spread across the lease after the concession. If you need an effective rent of 2,750 and the market expects one month free in twelve, the face rent must be 2,750 × 12 ÷ 11 = 3,000 a month. Ask whether 3,000 is a face rent tenants will accept. If comparable buildings are advertising 2,800 with one month free, their effective rent is 2,800 × 11 ÷ 12 = 2,566.67, and your 2,750 effective is about 7 percent above theirs. That is a fact to explain, not to hope away.

Part 3: From the loan maturity back to the lease-up pace

Absorption is the pace at which units are leased, net of move-outs, usually expressed as units per month. Now reverse engineer the calendar.

  • The construction loan matures 30 months after closing.
  • Construction takes 18 months to occupancy.
  • The permanent lender wants, as a hypothetical practice term, three months of operating history at stabilised occupancy before it will fund.
  • Stabilisation means 95 percent occupancy: 60 × 0.95 = 57 units leased.

Work backward from month 30. Subtract three months of operating history: the building must be stabilised by month 27. Subtract construction of 18 months: lease-up must take no more than 27 − 18 = 9 months. Required absorption: 57 units ÷ 9 months = 6.33 units a month.

Now check the market. If comparable new buildings leased at 6 units a month, the plan needs 57 ÷ 6 = 9.5 months, stabilises at month 27.5, and finishes its three months of history at month 30.5, a half month after the loan matures. The deal is half a month short on a perfect construction schedule. Any construction delay pushes it further.

Part 4: How sensitive the required rent is to the cap rate

The capitalisation rate at which the building will be valued is not yours to choose. Run the backward calculation again at a cap rate a quarter point higher, 5.25 percent. Required NOI = 28,200,000 × 0.0525 = 1,480,500. Add back 528,000: 2,008,500. Divide by 0.95: 2,114,211. Remove 60,000: 2,054,211. Divide by 720 unit-months: 2,853 a month. A quarter-point move in a number set by the market raised the rent the deal needs by about 103 dollars a month, nearly 4 percent. That is why reverse engineering is done at the cap rate you expect and at one a little worse.

Part 5: What the reverse engineering tells you to do

Three responses are available, and each has a cost.

  • Negotiate a construction loan extension option, perhaps six months, for a fee. That turns a cliff into a slope.
  • Start leasing before completion, from a show suite, to bank leases ahead of occupancy, if the local rules and your lender permit pre-leasing.
  • Offer larger concessions to lease faster, which lowers effective rent. Reverse engineer it: if two free months in twelve are needed, effective rent at a face of 3,000 becomes 3,000 × 10 ÷ 12 = 2,500, and stabilised NOI falls. Calculate whether faster leasing is worth the lower rent at the refinance test.

Second worked example: the cost of the extension option. Suppose the lender charges a fee of 0.25 percent of the loan for a six-month extension, which is a hypothetical practice figure. On 15,275,000 that is 38,188, plus six months of interest at 7 percent on the full balance, 15,275,000 × 0.07 × 0.5 = 534,625, if you use it. The fee is cheap insurance. The interest is the real cost, and it belongs in the budget's delay case.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a calendar that only works if everything goes right. The control is to reverse engineer the absorption pace required to meet the loan maturity with the refinance conditions, compare it with the slowest credible comparable, and buy time with an extension option before you need it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner checks whether the rent is achievable but never checks whether it is achievable in time. A rent that arrives three months after the loan matures is worth much less than the same rent on schedule. Remember too that absorption is net: if ten leases are signed in a month and two tenants give notice, absorption that month is eight, not ten.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the outside view: base your forecast on what similar projects actually achieved, not on the details of your own plan. Absorption is the place to use it. Do not ask how fast your marketing will lease the building. Ask how fast the last five comparable buildings actually leased, and plan around the slower half.

Recap

Required value at the cap rate gives required NOI. Add back expenses and reserves, gross up for vacancy, and remove other income to find the required rent. Convert effective rent to face rent with concessions. Work back from loan maturity to the absorption pace required, and compare it with the market. Buy time before you need it.

Next: Remi in the room with the lender's appraiser, who thinks your rent is too high.
checklist: Compute required NOI from the target value and cap rate
Add back expenses and reserves, gross up for vacancy, remove other income
Convert required gross potential rent to a monthly rent per unit
Translate between face rent and effective rent with concessions
Work back from loan maturity to the required absorption pace
Compare required absorption with the slowest credible comparable
Price an extension option and the interest it would cost
head: Field checklist
speak: I run the pro forma backward. The deal needs a value of 28.2 million at a 5 percent cap rate, so it needs 1.41 million of NOI. Add back 528,000 of expenses and reserves for 1.938 million of effective gross income, divide by 95 percent for vacancy to get 2.04 million, remove 60,000 of other income, and the building needs 1.98 million of rent: 2,750 a month per unit, effective. With one month free, that's a face rent of 3,000. Then the calendar. The loan matures at month 30, the take-out lender wants three months of stabilised history, and construction takes 18 months, so 57 units must lease in 9 months: 6.3 a month. If comparables leased at 6, I am half a month short on a perfect schedule. So I negotiate an extension option now, while it is cheap.
terms: Absorption — the pace at which units are leased, net of move-outs, usually stated in units per month.
Concession — a discount given to attract a tenant, such as free rent at the start of a lease.
Face rent — the rent stated in the lease before concessions are taken into account.

hostile.q: Your lease-up needs 6.3 units a month. The last three buildings in this area averaged under 6. Why should we believe you?
hostile.a: You shouldn't, and the plan doesn't require you to. Our base case uses 5.5 units a month, below the comparable average, which stabilises at month 28.4. The construction loan carries a six-month extension option, so the refinance date is month 36 if we need it. The extension fee and interest are in the delay case in the budget. Faster leasing would be upside.

title: The appraiser thinks your rent is too high
summary: A scene with the lender's appraiser, whose market rent is 100 dollars lower than yours. This lesson gives the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, and when to stay silent, plus a monthly thread on keeping a decision journal.
body:
You cannot instruct an appraiser to agree with you. You can give them evidence they cannot responsibly ignore, and you can do it in a way that makes them want to look at it.

Recall

Q. In a budget review, why should you raise your weakest line yourself?

A. Because it shows the lender you know where the risk sits and will tell them before they find it, which makes everything else you say more credible.

Q. What is a capitalised interest cost?

A. Interest incurred during construction recorded as part of the asset's cost rather than as an expense, in reporting frameworks that permit it.

Q. What does "acknowledge, bridge, answer" mean?

A. Recognise the concern, connect it to what matters, then answer with evidence.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, on Day 3 you saw that a 100-dollar difference in monthly rent contributed to a refinance shortfall of nearly two million. The appraiser's rent is not a detail. It flows into the lender's NOI, the take-out loan, and your equity. An appraiser is a licensed professional bound by professional standards to give an independent opinion. Trying to pressure one is improper and, in many places, prohibited. What is proper, and expected, is to provide relevant market evidence the appraiser may not have.

The setting

This is a hypothetical scene. The lender's appraiser has issued a draft concluding market rent of 2,650 a month. Your pro forma uses 2,750. The lender has agreed to a call so you can share information. The appraiser is careful, busy, and has heard many developers argue rent.

Before the call

Read the draft and find the comparables it used. List them beside yours. Usually the gap comes from one of three places: the appraiser used asking rents rather than signed effective rents, used older buildings without adjusting for age and amenities, or weighted a large building whose unit mix differs from yours. Prepare evidence for the specific gap you find, not a general case that your rent is right.

The lines to say

Open with respect for their independence. Say: "Thank you for the call. I'm not asking you to change a conclusion. I'd like to make sure you have three signed leases that weren't in the comparable set, and the concession detail on two that were."

Then the evidence, specific and short. Say: "Comparable 4 in your draft is advertised at 2,600. We have its signed rent roll extract from the leasing broker: effective rent on the last six two-bedroom leases averages 2,690 after one month free. It also has no parking, and our units include a stall."

And the honest concession. Say: "Your comparable 2 is a fair point against us. It is newer and leases at 2,620. Our case is that it sits on an arterial road with no balconies. If that adjustment isn't supportable, I'd rather know now."

Say that out loud now.

The question behind the question

When the appraiser asks, "Have these leases been verified?", the question behind it is: will I be exposed if I rely on this? Answer that question. Say: "The two-bedroom figures come from the managing broker by email; I'll send it with their contact so you can confirm directly." You are making their verification easy, which is the most persuasive thing you can do.

The lines never to say

  • "The lender needs 2,750 for the loan to work." That is pressure, and it undermines everything else you say.
  • "Other appraisers have accepted our numbers." It invites the reply that this one is not other appraisers.
  • "Your comparables are wrong." Say which comparable, what fact, and what evidence.

When to stay silent

After you present the evidence, stop. Do not ask what they will conclude. They cannot tell you, and asking makes the call feel like pressure. If they push back on a comparable, let them finish. If they say they will consider it, thank them and end the call. The decision is theirs.

Worked example: what a partial win is worth

Suppose the final report concludes 2,700. Using Day 3's lender adjustments, 7 percent vacancy, expenses of 510,000 and reserves of 24,000, the lender's NOI becomes: gross potential rent 60 × 2,700 × 12 = 1,944,000; plus 60,000 other income, 2,004,000; less 7 percent vacancy of 140,280, 1,863,720; less 534,000, NOI 1,329,720. At 1.25 times coverage and a 7.73 percent constant, the take-out is about 1,329,720 ÷ 1.25 ÷ 0.0773 = 13,762,000, about 346,000 more than at 2,650. A 50-dollar change in the appraiser's rent moved your equity requirement by about a third of a million. That is why the call is worth preparing for, and why it must be done properly.

A second exchange

Suppose the appraiser replies: "Your three new leases are all from one building owned by your broker's client." The question behind it is whether the evidence is independent. Do not defend the broker. Say: "That's fair. Two of the three are from that building. I can add the effective rents from the public listings history for two other buildings, and I'd ask you to weight the broker's building as one comparable, not three." You have conceded the weakness, offered more evidence and proposed a reasonable weighting. That is how a professional disagreement is supposed to sound.

After the call

Send the lender, not the appraiser directly unless the lender has asked you to, a short email listing exactly what was shared and the sources for each item. That creates a record that the information was provided properly, and it gives the lender's credit officer the same evidence. Then stop. Do not follow up asking whether the appraiser has changed the figure. The final report will arrive when it arrives.

Holding your state

If the appraiser does not move, you will feel it. Do not show it on the call. Thank them, and in the next conversation with the lender, discuss structure, not the appraisal: a larger extension option, an earn-out tranche that funds when actual rents are proven, or a later refinance. A professional's independent conclusion is a fact you plan around.

Monthly thread: decision journals

Before a call like this, write three lines in a decision journal: what you expect the appraiser to conclude, how confident you are, and why. After the report arrives, write what happened. Over a few years you will see whether your rent judgements run high, which most developers' do, and by how much. That is your personal correction factor, and no consultant can give it to you.

A decision journal works because memory edits itself after the fact. Without a written prediction you will remember being more right than you were. Keep it short, dated and private, and review it at the end of each project.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pressuring an independent professional. It can breach rules, it damages your relationship with the lender, and it rarely works. The control is to provide evidence only, through proper channels, and to accept the conclusion.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner argues the conclusion instead of the comparables. Appraisers move on evidence about specific comparables, not on the developer's confidence. A second mistake is to bring twenty comparables when three good ones would do. Volume reads as an attempt to overwhelm rather than inform, and it buries your strongest evidence.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied Cialdini's principles of influence. The one that applies here is not liking or scarcity. It is reciprocity in its most professional form: you make the other person's job easier by supplying verified, organised evidence, and they give your evidence the attention it deserves.

Recap

Respect the appraiser's independence. Find the source of the gap before the call. Present specific evidence, concede fair points, make verification easy, then stop talking. Never use the lender's needs as an argument. Plan around the conclusion.

Next: Kema's review of the week, with a Red Pen drill on a flawed revenue block.
checklist: Read the appraiser's comparables and list them beside yours before the call
Identify the specific source of the rent gap
Bring signed effective rents, not asking rents, with sources
Offer the appraiser a direct way to verify each lease
Concede the fair points against you
Never cite the lender's needs as a reason for a higher rent
Write a prediction in your decision journal before the report arrives
head: Field checklist
speak: The lender's appraiser has 2,650 a month; my pro forma has 2,750. An appraiser is a licensed professional giving an independent opinion, so I never pressure them and never say the lender needs my number. Before the call I find the source of the gap, usually asking rents instead of signed effective rents, or older buildings not adjusted for age and amenities. On the call I say I'm not asking them to change a conclusion, I present three signed leases they didn't have and the concession detail on two they did, I concede the comparable that genuinely hurts me, and I give them a direct way to verify. Then I stop talking. If the report lands at 2,700 instead of 2,650, the take-out loan rises by about 346,000. If it doesn't move, I plan around it with structure: an extension, an earn-out, or a later refinance.
terms: Appraiser — a licensed professional who gives an independent opinion of a property's value.
Comparable — a similar property whose rent or sale price is used as evidence for the subject property.
Decision journal — a dated private record of a decision, the prediction behind it and the confidence level, reviewed later against the outcome.

hostile.q: Isn't sharing your own rent evidence with the appraiser just a way of pressuring them?
hostile.a: No, as long as it stays evidence. I'm supplying signed effective rents with sources and a direct contact so they can verify them, through the lender's channel, and I'm conceding the comparable that cuts against us. I am not discussing the loan amount or what conclusion would help. The appraiser decides what weight to give the evidence, and I plan around whatever they conclude.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 14 review: revenue, vacancy and stabilised NOI
summary: Six questions and answers on the revenue side of the pro forma, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a flawed revenue block, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one idea: revenue is the softest number in a pro forma and the one with the greatest effect on value, so it must be evidenced, legal and on time.

Recall

Q. What is the biggest risk in a budget review with a lender?

A. Defending a number you privately doubt. The control is to list your three weakest lines in advance and raise the worst one yourself.

Q. In owner reporting, what is the difference between budget and forecast?

A. The budget is the approved baseline. The forecast is the current best estimate of the final figure. The gap between them is what a report must explain.

Q. What is the right response to a number you do not know in a meeting?

A. Do not guess. Commit to a time to confirm it, and deliver on that time.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, say each answer aloud before reading it. Retrieval fixes the idea; rereading only feels as though it does.

The six questions

Question 1. Walk the revenue staircase. Answer: gross potential rent, plus other income, gives potential gross income; minus vacancy and credit loss gives effective gross income; minus operating expenses and reserves gives net operating income.

Question 2. Why does a 5 percent rent error cause a larger NOI error? Answer: because operating expenses are largely fixed. Lost rent comes straight off NOI, so NOI falls proportionally more, and development profit, a thin slice above cost, falls far more. In the week's example, a 5 percent rent drop cut profit by 40 percent.

Question 3. State Rule 14. Answer: I underwrite revenue only from rents I can legally charge and have evidence tenants pay today; any increase that depends on a change in law, regulation or tenancy is shown as upside, never as base case.

Question 4. How does a lender rebuild your NOI? Answer: lower rent, from in-place rents or its appraiser; higher vacancy; a management fee and its own expense minimums; and larger reserves. It then sizes the take-out loan on the binding test, usually debt service coverage.

Question 5. Why does property tax often rise after completion? Answer: because the completed building is reassessed at a higher value. A tax line copied from the construction period understates operating expenses.

Question 6. A loan matures at month 30, construction takes 18 months, the take-out needs three months of stabilised history, and 57 units must lease. What absorption is required? Answer: stabilise by month 27, so 9 months of lease-up, so 57 ÷ 9 = 6.33 units a month.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Day 1 built the staircase from gross potential rent to stabilised NOI and showed operating leverage. Day 2 took Stuyvesant Town apart: a base case that counted rents the law did not yet allow, financed with debt that left no room for delay. Day 3 showed the lender's NOI and the refinance shortfall it creates. Day 4 covered rent regulation, tenancy law, use restrictions and property tax. Day 5 reverse engineered the rent and the lease-up pace from the value and the loan maturity. Day 6 put you on a call with the appraiser.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical revenue block and find the defects before reading on.

40 units at asking rent of 2,900 a month: gross potential rent 1,392,000. Other income: 40 parking stalls at 150 a month, 72,000. Vacancy 3 percent of rent: 41,760. Effective gross income 1,422,240. Operating expenses 380,000, owner to self-manage. Rents grow 6 percent a year from year 1, including during lease-up. Stabilised NOI 1,042,240. Value at 4.5 percent cap: 23,160,889. Property tax per seller's current bill.

The defects:

  1. Asking rent, not effective rent. Underwriting should use signed effective rents after concessions.
  2. Other income at 100 percent occupancy. Vacancy is applied to rent only, while parking is assumed fully let. Apply vacancy to potential gross income, or justify the parking separately.
  3. No management fee and no replacement reserve. Self-management does not remove the cost; a lender will add a fee, and reserves are missing entirely.
  4. Rent growth of 6 percent a year, including during lease-up, with no check against rent regulation. During lease-up, rents usually come with concessions, not increases.
  5. Property tax from the seller's bill, which will not reflect the completed building's assessment.
  6. A precision trap. Value stated to the dollar, 23,160,889, implies an accuracy no pro forma has. Round it.

Find five of six for this week's standard.

Now quantify one correction. Apply 5 percent vacancy to potential gross income of 1,464,000: 73,200, giving effective gross income of 1,390,800. Add a management fee of 3.5 percent, 48,678, and reserves of 300 per unit, 12,000. NOI becomes 1,390,800 − 380,000 − 48,678 − 12,000 = 950,122, about 9 percent below the stated 1,042,240, before any correction to rent, growth or tax. At the same 4.5 percent cap rate, value falls by about two million.

Boardroom drill

Explain the revenue side of a pro forma to a non-specialist board in two minutes. Stand, time yourself, then compare.

Model answer: "Our building is worth what it earns. Sixty apartments at 2,750 a month, which is the effective rent tenants are paying today in ten comparable buildings, gives 1.98 million a year if every unit is full. Add 60,000 from parking and storage. Then we assume 5 percent of that is lost to empty units and unpaid rent, so we collect about 1.94 million. Running the building, taxes, insurance, repairs, staff and management, costs 510,000, and we set aside 18,000 a year for things that wear out. What's left, 1.41 million, is our net operating income. Buyers pay about 20 times that for a building like this, so it's worth about 28.2 million against a cost of 23.5. Two cautions. If rents are 5 percent lower, our profit falls by 40 percent, so we have tested that case. And our lender believes the income is about 8 percent lower, which leaves a gap of about 1.9 million when we refinance, which our equity commitment already covers."

The biggest risk

The biggest risk after this week is trusting a revenue number because it is tidy. The control is to ask three questions of every rent: is it effective, is it legal, and can it arrive before the loan matures? Write those three questions at the top of the revenue tab in every pro forma you own, so that the next person who edits it sees them too.

The beginner's mistake

A second mistake is to treat this review as complete once the answers are right. Return to Question 6 in a week and work it again from a blank page, changing one number, such as a 24-month loan or 50 units. Being able to rebuild the calculation with new inputs is the test of understanding; remembering the answer is not.

The beginner tests costs to the dollar and accepts revenue on a broker's word. Revenue deserves at least as much evidence as costs, because it drives value through a multiplier.

Callback

In Week 13, Rule 13 required every estimate to travel with its class, date, scope and contingency. Revenue deserves the same treatment: every rent assumption should travel with its source, its date, whether it is effective or asking, and whether it depends on a change that has not yet happened. Rules 13 and 14 together cover both sides of the pro forma.

Recap

Revenue steps down from gross potential rent to stabilised NOI. Small rent errors become large profit errors. Base-case revenue must be legal and evidenced. The lender's NOI is lower than yours and sets the take-out. Rules shape rent and tax. Reverse engineer the rent and the calendar.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was revenue. The staircase runs from gross potential rent, plus other income, minus vacancy and credit loss, to effective gross income, then minus operating expenses and reserves to stabilised net operating income. Because expenses are largely fixed, a 5 percent rent error became a 6.7 percent value error and a 40 percent profit error. Stuyvesant Town showed what happens when base-case revenue includes rents the law doesn't yet allow, which gave me Rule 14: base-case revenue comes only from rents I can legally charge and evidence today. A lender rebuilds my NOI lower, and that sets a take-out loan that may not repay the construction loan. Rent regulation, tenancy law, use restrictions and property tax all shape the lines. And I reverse engineer the rent and the lease-up pace from the value and the loan maturity. Three questions for every rent: effective, legal, on time.
terms: Operating leverage — the effect by which, because expenses are largely fixed, a change in revenue causes a proportionally larger change in net operating income.
Refinance shortfall — the gap between a construction loan to be repaid and the smaller permanent loan available to repay it.
Effective rent — the average rent actually paid over a lease after concessions such as free months.

hostile.q: Your pro forma has vacancy of 3 percent applied only to rent. Why should I accept that?
hostile.a: You shouldn't. That was a defect in the draft. The revised block applies 5 percent vacancy and credit loss to all potential gross income, including parking, adds a 3.5 percent management fee and 300 per unit of reserves, and uses signed effective rents. NOI falls about 9 percent from the draft, and the value and the refinance test are rerun on the revised figure.
